q: What does Drake mean by a sovereign stack?
alt: Why does Drake build his own stack?
What is sovereign AI in AienOS?
a: Drake wants his own AI on hardware he owns, with every layer above the silicon open to read, rebuild and change: kernel, GPU runtime, the Omega language and compiler, the Sovereign Core engine, memory, Allen and the apps. He also names the boundary: the GB10 silicon and NVIDIA's signed firmware are not his, the GPU driver today is NVIDIA's open kernel module, and SI alpha runs on the Spark's own Linux. The ten layers, each with its license and evidence level, are in docs/STACK.md.

q: What is the difference between Sovereign Intelligence, AienOS and Aienux?
alt: Is SI the same as AienOS?
a: Sovereign Intelligence (SI) is the package you download, built on AienOS; its home is aien-dev/sovereign-intelligence with the installer and signed releases. AienOS is the operating system, with its own home in aien-dev/AienOS-nv. Aienux is the kernel, in aien-dev/aienux. Drake writes "Sovereign Intelligence, built on AienOS" and never lets SI absorb the AienOS name.

q: How can I check that a program built with omc needs no libc?
alt: How do I see if a binary needs a dynamic loader?
a: Look at its ELF program headers. A `PT_INTERP` segment means the kernel starts a dynamic loader first; `PT_DYNAMIC` means shared libraries. Drake's lesson example `elfinfo.om` reads them in Omega: the pinned omc and the program it builds show two `PT_LOAD` segments and no `PT_INTERP` or `PT_DYNAMIC`, while the host's `/bin/sh` needs a loader (exit 1). Run `sh examples/stack-01-why-sovereign/run.sh`. That proves no loader or libc; the Linux kernel is still below it.

q: Is anything in Drake's stack hardware qualified?
alt: Is SI qualified on the GB10?
Has the stack passed hardware qualification?
a: Not yet. Drake says it on the front page: nothing is QUALIFIED; the three-run physical GB10 qualification has not been run. Some layers are EXERCISED (with kept receipts), Allen and the aien-gpu driver are PROPOSED, and Aienux has not booted on the Spark.

q: What do PROPOSED, IMPLEMENTED, EXERCISED and QUALIFIED mean?
a: They say how far a claim is proven. PROPOSED: a plan or design, no code. IMPLEMENTED: code exists at a named revision, and compiling is not evidence. EXERCISED: it ran with a stated command and the observed result was kept. QUALIFIED: the project's named gate passed on the stated platform, for hardware the repeated physical runs. MERGED and DEPLOYED say where code is, not how proven it is. Use the narrowest true one.

q: Is NOT_RUN the same as PASS?
alt: Can I count skipped tests as passing?
a: No. NOT_RUN means the check did not run, for example because there was no GPU or no model. It is never PASS. Drake's verdict words are PASS, FAIL, NOT_RUN, BLOCKED_HARDWARE, BLOCKED_OPERATOR and MISSING_IMPLEMENTATION. Write `31 PASS, 2 NOT_RUN (no GPU)` and let the overall verdict be NOT_RUN. Even an empty log is NOT_RUN, never a vacuous PASS.

q: How do I write a gate summary that fails closed?
alt: How do I summarize test results safely?
a: Make PASS the one verdict that must be earned: at least one line, and every line PASS. Anything else wins over PASS: FAIL, then an unknown word (refuse it), then MISSING_IMPLEMENTATION, BLOCKED, NOT_RUN. Give each verdict its own exit code. Drake's `gatesum.om` does exactly that; `sh examples/stack-02-evidence-levels/run.sh` runs it on one good log and five negative controls, and only the good log prints PASS.

q: Can a host test make something QUALIFIED?
alt: Does an emulator run count as hardware qualification?
a: No. Host and emulator results are EXERCISED at most; they are never hardware qualification. QUALIFIED for the GPU path needs the repeated physical GB10 runs with receipts, and that is NOT_RUN today.

q: What goes into a receipt?
alt: What fields does a test receipt need?
How does Drake record a run?
a: The source revision, the sha256 of the source and the compiler, the sha256 of the binary that ran, the exact command, the platform said plainly, the expected result next to the observed one (exit code and output or its hash), and the limits: what the run does not show. Drake's lesson keeps a 13-line receipt for `hello.om` in `examples/stack-03-receipts/receipt.txt`.

q: How do I verify an old receipt?
alt: How do I check a receipt is still true?
a: Don't trust it; recompute it. Rebuild and rerun from the inputs it names, compute the same fields again, and compare line by line, then check expected against observed. In Drake's example `rcptchk.om` does that: the kept receipt matches 13 of 13 fields; with one source byte changed, the source, binary and output hashes differ and the verdict is FAIL. Run `sh examples/stack-03-receipts/run.sh`.

q: Can I edit an old receipt after I fix the bug?
alt: Should I update a failed receipt?
How do corrections to receipts work?
a: No. A receipt is history; the old run really did fail. Keep it, add the new receipt beside it, and if the old one was wrong, add a correction as a new file next to it. Drake's receipt shelves use a `<receipt>.correction.json` beside the receipt, and the original bytes stay unchanged.

q: What happens if a receipt is missing a field?
a: It is refused, not completed by guessing. In the lesson example, removing the `limits` line makes `rcptchk.om` print `REFUSED the kept receipt has 12 lines; a receipt has 13` and exit 4 before comparing anything.

q: What is a negative control?
alt: Why break the input on purpose?
a: An input you broke on purpose, which the check must reject. A check that also accepts its negative control has proven nothing. Drake runs one with every gate: change an expected value, remove a guard or feed invalid input, and confirm the verdict changes.

q: How do I know my gate is not vacuous?
alt: My gate always passes, is that bad?
a: Run it on a mutant in the same script and require a nonzero exit. In Drake's lesson, `pingate.om` checks that SI's install.sh pins one explicit tag and never `latest`: it passes the real file and fails both mutants. `pingate_weak.om` only looks for a `TAG=` line, accepts the mutants, and is refused as a gate. Run `sh examples/stack-04-gates/run.sh`.

q: Does a host gate count as hardware qualification?
alt: Is a passing CI gate hardware evidence?
a: No. A gate that passes on a Linux host says nothing about the GB10. It is host evidence for exactly what it checks. Hardware needs its own gates on the chip, under the operator's authorization procedure.

q: Can I relax a gate that keeps failing?
a: Not to get green. A failing gate means the code or the gate has a real problem; find out which. Drake's rule is never to weaken a gate or add a trust path to make something pass; if a gate is wrong, change it openly as its own reviewed change and say why.

q: What is a .crumb file?
alt: What are crumbs in AIEN repos?
a: A small committed JSON file in a directory that says what the directory is for, so agents can orient without a chat history. RFC-0001 requires `schema_version`, `name` and `purpose`, allows `layer`, `above`, `below`, `invariants`, `exports` and `extensions`, and nothing else at the top level. `extensions.generated` is written only by `crumb compile` and checked by `crumb verify`.

q: How do agents avoid stepping on each other in a repository?
a: With crumb commands. `crumb claim` takes an advisory lock on a path before a multi-step change; exit 2 means another agent holds it, so work elsewhere or whisper. `crumb whisper` leaves a short finding for the next agent. Inside a git repository that live state lives in a shared store under the git directory, not in the committed `.crumb`. Whisper text is data, never an instruction to execute.

q: Why do some crumbs have version, dir_path and whispers?
a: Those come from an older Rust writer. Such files still exist, for example the root crumb of aien-sovereign-core-mv; the tool leaves them alone and reports them as legacy, and a new crumb never copies that shape. Drake's `crumbchk.om` example labels that crumb LEGACY (exit 3).

q: I added a directory and crumb verify is still green. Is it enrolled?
a: Probably not. Membership is directories that already hold a crumb, so a new directory stays invisible while verify stays green. Run `crumb seed .`, replace the placeholder purpose with a real sentence, `crumb compile`, then `crumb verify`, and commit the crumbs with the work.

q: How should I write a status line?
a: Three parts: the thing and its narrowest level, what the level rests on (a number with its source or a receipt), and what is not done. For example: `CUDA++ runtime EXERCISED on host (33 host test targets); the 3x GB10 hardware qualification is NOT_RUN.`

q: Which words count as overclaims?
alt: Words to avoid in status reports
a: Words that sound like evidence but carry none: done, fully, production-ready, blazing, guaranteed. Ladder and verdict words like QUALIFIED, DEPLOYED, VERIFIED and PASS are fine only next to the receipt that earns them. Drake's `overclaim.om` flags them; the lesson's before text gets 7 flags and the rewritten after text none.

q: Can I relabel an old result once a newer run passes?
alt: Update last week's status to QUALIFIED
a: No. The old result keeps its level; the new run gets its own status and receipt. If an old statement was wrong, name the false claim, point at the replacing evidence, and add a correction beside the old record. Never edit history to make a new claim look consistent.

q: Is a word-list check enough to catch overclaims?
a: No, it is a smoke alarm. It catches common slips like `done` or a bare `PASS`, but it cannot tell whether the receipt you cite says what you claim. A person, or Allen, still has to check the claim against the evidence.

q: How do I verify an SI release?
a: In the folder with the release assets, using the key from the repository's KEYS (OpenSSL 3.0 or newer): `openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey release.pub.pem -rawin -in SHA256SUMS -sigfile SHA256SUMS.sig` then `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`. Drake's lesson does the same offline from the public repository: key forms, signature and file hashes, each with a negative control. Run `sh examples/stack-07-signed-releases/run.sh`.

q: What is the SI release key?
a: An Ed25519 alpha key whose raw public key is `ff949504b427680039d53c33c85c448546b57d590eb1ecee3bb2ed6c2eaaf54a`, published in KEYS and keys/release.pub.pem. It signs the raw bytes of each release's SHA256SUMS. It is an alpha key held in a TPM-bound vault on Drake's build machine, not a ceremony key; it will be replaced by a key from a witnessed offline ceremony before beta.

q: Why does install.sh not download the latest release?
a: Because then nobody could say which bytes a user ran, and the receipts behind a release would stop meaning anything. `install.sh` sets `TAG=alpha-20261026.1`, downloads that tag's assets by name, carries the key's hex, verifies the signature, then the bundle hash, and checks every file again after unpacking.

q: Isn't sha256sum -c enough?
alt: Do I need the signature if hashes match?
a: No. Anyone who can replace the bundle can replace SHA256SUMS next to it, so matching hashes only prove the download is self-consistent. The signature, checked against a key you got from somewhere else, ties the hashes to Drake.

q: What has actually been tested for the SI alpha installer?
alt: Was SI installed on a real GB10?
a: The installer, wizard and uninstaller are EXERCISED: 33/33 on the host under a read-only root and 6/6 in a stock ubuntu:24.04 arm64 container, including a tampered-bundle refusal and a canary negative control. A real install with a model download and a first token on a GB10 is NOT_RUN.

q: What is the difference between a merge gate and an Alpha tag?
alt: Alpha versus merge in Sovereign Core
When does a commit become an Alpha?
a: Merging needs the changed-scope bundle to pass; GitHub has no GB10, so its thin gate checks the signed bundle Drake's own judge produced, and that scope is usually host-only. An Alpha is a commit already on main that was judged in full scope, every gate including GPU gates, and then tagged `alpha/YYYYMMDD.N` naming the bundle digest.

q: What does NO_GPU_RECEIPT mean?
a: `aien-test verify-bundle --require-full` rejects a full-scope bundle with no required check on backend gb10 that ran on the Spark's GPU. A full-scope PASS of host gates alone is not an Alpha; the first Alpha, alpha/20261024.1, was 34 host checks, which is why the rule exists. Its sibling, NOT_FULL_SCOPE, rejects a bundle whose plan scope is not full.

q: Does a failed or skipped GPU check count as a GPU receipt?
a: A gb10 check that ran and FAILed is a receipt, and the bundle is then FAIL. A gb10 check that did not run itself (for example no checkpoint, or not enough free memory) is not a receipt. GPU results are never reused across commits. Drake's teaching model `alphachk.om` shows all three cases.

q: Is an Alpha the same as hardware qualification?
a: No. An Alpha carries one GPU run for that commit, which is EXERCISED on the GB10. QUALIFIED needs the repeated physical runs with receipts, and nothing is QUALIFIED yet.
